title: AI Strategist: Strategy and Business Value
description: Domain 2 (28%): use cases, build-buy-partner, prioritizing and stopping initiatives, when AI is the wrong tool, KPIs, baselines, ROI, cost, and competitive positioning.

cards.definition: Start from the business or customer problem and the result you want, then ask whether and how AI helps, rather than starting from the technology.

example.text: A sales leader asks for 'an AI tool'. The strategist first pins down the outcome that matters, faster and better-targeted proposals, and only then picks the AI capability that serves it.

cards.definition: Tying each AI capability to a measurable business outcome, such as reduced business risk, better ESG performance, revenue growth, or operational efficiency.

example.text: Spotting faulty parts on a production line maps to reduced business risk. Personalized product recommendations map to revenue growth, and auto-coding travel receipts maps to operational efficiency.

cards.definition: Choosing to buy a ready-made AI product, build or customize your own, or bring in a partner, weighed on budget, timelines, in-house skills, vendor proposals, and compliance.

example.text: A firm with no ML staff wants a document assistant this year. It customizes an existing model rather than creating one from scratch, and pushes back on the 'not invented here' urge to rebuild what already exists.

cards.definition: Adopting a ready-made AI application: least in-house build effort, but you take a buyer's view and rely on the vendor's enterprise agreement and data terms.
Developing or customizing your own AI solution: more control over data and fit, but a builder's view, with more responsibility for protecting data and threat modeling.
Bringing in outside specialists, such as AWS Partners, AWS Professional Services or the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, to co-build a proof of concept, support you, and transfer knowledge.
AWS's catalog for buying pre-built AI agents, agent tools, software with AI built in, and partner professional services: a ready shelf for buy and partner choices.
A grid that ranks candidate AI initiatives by business impact, feasibility, and alignment with strategic goals, so the top few get funded first.

example.text: A workshop produces ten AI ideas. Scored on impact, feasibility, and fit with company goals, two rise to the top and become the first proofs of concept with their own budget.

cards.definition: Whether an initiative can keep delivering value over time rather than a one-off win; AWS also uses 'sustainability' for environmental impact, a different idea.
The portfolio call at each checkpoint: scale what proves value, pause what isn't ready yet, and stop what will not deliver, moving the money to better bets.

example.text: One pilot hits its targets and is expanded. Another isn't ready yet, so it is put on hold. A third shows no business gain, so it is stopped and its budget goes to the next idea.

cards.term: When AI is not the right solution
cards.definition: Choose AI only for a clear, substantial benefit; if ordinary software or a manual process would do, or reliable examples to build and test it are lacking, reframe or pick another solution.
What to plan before moving a process onto AI or between AI platforms: business continuity, cost implications, data readiness, and performance impact.
Bedrock models move from Active to Legacy to End-of-Life; check the model card's EOL dates and plan migration before EOL, because nothing migrates automatically.
Running the old process alongside the new AI-based one until the AI proves it meets quality and performance targets, keeping a fallback for business continuity.
Hard gains that are measurable in the short term, such as cost reduction and revenue growth.
Real but harder-to-measure gains that often show up over the longer term, such as customer satisfaction and employee productivity.
A business measure of an AI initiative's success; AWS guidance says every technical metric should trace to a meaningful business outcome.
A measurement of the process before AI touches it, so the change after adoption can be proven rather than assumed.

example.text: A team fixed 5 bugs a week before AI and 15 after. Only the 10 extra count as AI's effect, and that is impossible to show without the 'before' number.

cards.definition: An early signal that predicts whether an AI initiative will succeed, such as adoption, repeat usage, task completion, and user satisfaction, seen before financial results.
A measure that confirms results after the fact, such as revenue growth, cost savings, or ROI; it proves value but arrives too late to steer early.
What each AI-driven outcome is worth against what it costs, recalculated at regular intervals rather than estimated once.
AI cost divided by a business value metric, such as cost per bug fixed; AWS calls it the building block for ROI, not ROI itself.
Direct AI service costs plus indirect ones: storage and vector databases, data transfer, monitoring and reporting, and agent calls to other services.
Hours saved count as value only when someone commits to turning them into a business result; otherwise the freed capacity is quietly absorbed.
Paying only for what you use, such as on-demand model calls on Amazon Bedrock, with no cost while the application sits idle.

example.text: With usage hard to predict, a finance leader avoids long, fixed-quantity contracts and picks consumption-based pricing, so spend can grow with adoption and shrink as efficiency improves.

cards.definition: Paying for the compute instances you run by the hour, such as Amazon SageMaker AI training and inference instances; Savings Plans can lower the rate.
A set price per user per month, such as Amazon Quick's Plus plan, so cost grows with the number of users.
A 1- or 3-year commitment to a set amount of compute usage per hour in exchange for lower prices, including SageMaker AI Savings Plans.
A free AWS tool for estimating costs before you build; no AWS experience needed, and estimates can be saved or exported to share.
Early AI spend is mostly fixed foundation cost: data readiness, integration, governance, upskilling. Later, usage grows, unit costs fall, and spend ties to business impact.

example.text: In year one a firm spends most of its AI budget on data preparation, security, and training, with compute only 10–15%. As adoption grows, total spend rises but cost per outcome drops.

cards.definition: How far AI is already used across your industry; the further competitors have gone, the higher the cost of waiting and the stronger the case to invest more.
As AI spreads, customers raise their expectations of products and services, and AI-powered capabilities become part of what they expect.
Starting early builds experience, an AI-ready culture, and a talent pool that later entrants must catch up on.
Data you own that is rare and costly for others to acquire, so the AI products built on it are hard to copy.

example.text: Two insurers use the same foundation model. The one with decades of its own claims data and its adjusters' know-how gets better results, because the model alone is not a differentiator.

cards.definition: A self-reinforcing cycle: quality data trains an AI system, its predictions improve outcomes, deeper customer relationships follow, and they produce more data.
Using AI to do today's work faster or cheaper versus redesigning the process or business model; AWS research finds most firms still fix AI, not the process around it.
CAF-AI's Product domain: reimagining the business model by creating new value propositions (products, services) and revenue models that use AI.

example.text: A retailer stops at using AI to cut support costs, while a rival launches a paid personalized styling service built on AI. The first optimizes; the second transforms its business model.
